sections.history: Tiruppainjeeli lies a short way north of Tiruchirappalli, in the fertile country north of the Kaveri, and is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the Shiva temples sung by the Tevaram saints. Its name comes from the gneeli, a variety of plantain, for the place is remembered as an ancient grove of these trees; the Lord is accordingly Neelivaneswarar, he of the plantain forest. Tradition also calls the town the southern Kailash, holding that it broke away from the sacred mountain itself. The cave-like sanctum is traditionally credited to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I in about the seventh century, a dating that rests on tradition rather than a firm record, while inscriptions of the great Chola kings Rajaraja I and Rajendra I show the temple was already honoured and endowed in the early eleventh century.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, behind which rises a second, unfinished gopuram of the kind Tamil devotees call a mottai gopuram, a reminder of a tower that was never completed. The sanctum is unusual: it is built in the manner of a cave, set about six feet below the level of the courtyard, and is crowned by a two-tiered vimana. Nine steps climbing from the second gopuram are honoured as the nine planets, so the temple keeps no separate Navagraha shrine. Within the enclosure stand the shrine of the goddess Visalakshi, a shrine of Vishnu as Senthamarai Kannan, a small sanctum for Yama, and the shrine of Chotrudai Eswarar, the Lord of the Meal, linked to the story of Appar.
sections.legends: The temple's best-loved legend concerns Yama. When the boy Markandeya clung to the linga at Tirukkadaiyur, Shiva rose to protect him and struck down Yama, and with the lord of death gone the world was thrown out of its order. Bhudevi, Vishnu, Brahma and the other gods came to Shiva and begged that Yama be restored. At Tiruppainjeeli Shiva raised him, and tradition tells that Yama came forth through an opening in the earth on the day of Thai Poosam. He is shown here as a small child at the Lord's feet, and Vishnu, who pleaded on his behalf, is honoured in his own shrine. A second story belongs to the saint Appar, who, weary and hungry on his pilgrim road, was met by Shiva in the form of a Brahmin, fed, and guided to the temple, where the Lord revealed himself as a linga. That linga is worshipped as Chotrudai Eswarar to this day.
sections.festivals: Thai Poosam, in January or February, is the most distinctive day, with special worship offered to Yama in remembrance of his restoration. A ten-day Brahmotsavam fills the month of Chithirai, in April and May, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept as at every Shiva temple. Because the shrine is so closely bound to the thought of long life, families also come to offer prayers for sixtieth and eightieth birthdays. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruppainjeeli suits a quiet, unhurried visit. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram and climb the nine steps, then descend into the cool, low sanctum of Neelivaneswarar, which feels very much like entering an ancient cave. Spend a moment at the shrine of Chotrudai Eswarar and at the small Yama sanctum, where many elders come to pray for good health and a long life, before turning to Visalakshi in her own shrine. The village is rural and the pace gentle, and the Vishnu temple of Tiruvellarai is only about four kilometres away, so the two are often visited together.

visit.timings: Generally open from early morning until about midday and again from late afternoon until about eight in the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple lies about 15 to 20 km north of Tiruchirappalli by road, by way of Manachanallur, and is served by regular buses from the Chathiram bus stand in Tiruchirappalli. Uttamarkoil is the nearest railway station, a few kilometres away, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport is roughly 28 km distant. The Divya Desam temple of Tiruvellarai is about 4 km from here.
